questions.question: Which security mechanism controls record-level access to data in ServiceNow?

options.text: Roles
Groups
Access Control Lists (ACLs)
Data Policies

explanation.correct: Access Control Lists (ACLs) control record-level and field-level access to data. ACLs specify what tables, fields, and operations users can access based on roles and conditions. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Roles grant access to application modules and menus, but ACLs control the actual data access.
Groups organize users and can be assigned roles, but they don't directly control data access.
Data Policies enforce data integrity rules on forms, not access control.

source.excerpt: Most security settings are implemented using access controls. In addition to restricting CRUD operations, access control rules can restrict ServiceNow specific operations on tables and fields.

questions.question: Which elements does every access control list (ACL) specify? (Choose three.)

options.text: The decision type, rule type, and operation
The object being secured
The conditions required to access the object
The update set it was created in
The form view it applies to

explanation.correct: Every ACL specifies the decision type, rule type, and operation that define it; the object being secured; and the conditions required to access the object. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Update sets capture changes but aren't part of an ACL's definition.
ACLs secure objects and operations, not form views.

source.excerpt: The decision type, rule type and operation which defines the ACL … The object being secured … The conditions required to access the object

questions.question: An ACL on the Incident table requires the itil role and also has the data condition [Incident state] [is not] [Closed]. A user with itil tries to update a closed incident. What happens?

options.text: Access is denied, because a user must pass all conditions in an access control
Access is granted, because the user has the required role
Access is granted only for read
The data condition is ignored when a role is listed

explanation.correct: To gain access to an object and operation, a user must pass all the conditions listed in an access control, such as the required roles, security attributes, data conditions, and script. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The role alone isn't enough; every condition must pass.
This ACL governs updates; read access depends on read ACLs.
Data conditions are always evaluated along with roles.

source.excerpt: To gain access to an object and operation, a user must pass all conditions listed in an access control.

questions.question: What does the ACL engine do by default when an ACL is empty or invalid, such as having no role, security attribute, or data condition?

options.text: It completely denies access
It grants access to all authenticated users
It grants access to admins only
It ignores the ACL

explanation.correct: By default, the ACL engine completely denies access if an ACL is empty or invalid. Empty ACLs are ACLs without a defined role, security attribute, or data condition. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Empty ACLs deny access; they don't grant it.
The deny-by-default behavior isn't limited to non-admins in this description.
Empty ACLs are enforced as a deny.

source.excerpt: By default the ACL engine completely denies access if an ACL is empty or invalid.

questions.question: For the same object, there is an Allow-If ACL and a Deny-Unless ACL. Which is evaluated first?

options.text: The Deny-Unless ACL, which takes priority over Allow-If ACLs
The Allow-If ACL
Whichever ACL was created most recently
Both are evaluated in alphabetical order

explanation.correct: Deny-Unless ACLs take priority over Allow-If ACLs in ACL evaluation because they are evaluated first. Deny-Unless restricts access unless conditions pass; Allow-If allows access if conditions pass. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/acl-denial-behavior.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Allow-If is evaluated after Deny-Unless.
Creation date doesn't affect ACL evaluation order.
ACL evaluation isn't alphabetical.

source.excerpt: Deny-Unless ACLs will take priority against Allow-If ACLs in ACL Evaluation, as it will be evaluated first.

questions.question: A user passes the field ACL for incident.short_description but fails every table ACL for the Incident table. What can they access?

options.text: No fields on the Incident table
Only the short_description field
All fields except short_description
All fields, because field ACLs override table ACLs

explanation.correct: A user must pass both table and field ACLs to access a record object. If they fail the table ACL, they are denied access to all fields in the table, even if they pass a field ACL. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/acl-rule-types.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Failing the table ACL blocks all fields.
Failing the table ACL blocks all fields, including this one.
Field ACLs don't override table ACLs.

source.excerpt: If a user fails a table ACL, the user is denied access to all fields in the table, even if the user passes a field ACL.

questions.question: ACLs exist on the Task table. How do they affect the Incident table, which extends Task?

options.text: ACLs for parent tables apply to any table that extends the parent table
They don't apply; each table needs its own ACLs
They apply only to fields added on the Incident table
They apply only if the admin enables inheritance per ACL

explanation.correct: If other tables extend a table, it's a parent table. ACLs for parent tables apply to any table that extends them, and ACLs for fields on a parent table apply to tables that extend it. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/acl-rule-types.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Child tables are covered by parent table ACLs.
Parent ACLs apply to inherited fields and records.
Inheritance is automatic, not a per-ACL option.

source.excerpt: ACLs for parent tables apply to any table that extends the parent table.

questions.question: Which role must you elevate to before you can create an ACL?

options.text: security_admin
admin
acl_admin
user_admin

explanation.correct: To create ACLs, you must elevate privileges to the security_admin role. Then navigate to System Security > Access Control (ACL) and select New. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/t_CreateAnACLRule.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Admin alone isn't enough; you must elevate to security_admin.
acl_admin isn't the role named in the procedure.
user_admin manages users and groups.

source.excerpt: To create ACLs, you must elevate privileges to the security_admin role.

questions.question: An administrator needs to secure both read and write operations on a custom table. How many ACLs are needed at minimum?

options.text: Two, because an ACL can only secure one operation
One ACL with both operations selected
One table ACL, which covers all operations automatically
None, because tables are open by default

explanation.correct: Each ACL secures one operation. To secure multiple operations, create a separate ACL for each. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/t_CreateAnACLRule.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: An ACL can't secure more than one operation.
A table ACL secures only the operation it defines.
The platform denies by default; ACLs grant access.

source.excerpt: An ACL can only secure one operation. To secure multiple operations, create a separate ACL for each.

questions.question: What is the effect of selecting Admin overrides on an ACL?

options.text: Users with the admin role automatically pass the permissions check for that ACL
Only admins can pass the ACL
The ACL is ignored for all users
Admins must meet the ACL's script conditions

explanation.correct: With Admin overrides selected, users with the admin role automatically pass the permissions check regardless of script or role restrictions. The nobody role, which only ServiceNow personnel can assign, takes precedence over admin override. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/t_CreateAnACLRule.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Admin overrides doesn't restrict the ACL to admins.
The ACL still applies to non-admin users.
That describes clearing the check box.

source.excerpt: Select this check box to have users with the admin role automatically pass the permissions check for this ACL.

questions.question: Which statements about elevated privilege roles are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: You don't have elevated privilege roles when you log in; you must manually elevate
An elevated role lasts only for the current session; timeout or logout removes it
Elevated roles are automatically granted to all admins at login
Elevated roles never expire once activated

explanation.correct: By default you don't have elevated privilege roles when you log in and must manually elevate. An elevated role lasts only for your user session; session timeout or logout removes it. In the base system, security_admin is the only elevated privilege role. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/c_ElevatedPrivilege.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Elevation is always manual.
Elevation ends with the session.

source.excerpt: By default, you do not have elevated privilege roles upon login. … An elevated privilege role lasts only for the duration of your user session.

questions.question: In the base system, which role is the only role with elevated privileges?

options.text: security_admin
admin
impersonator
itil_admin

explanation.correct: In the base system, security_admin is the only role with elevated privileges. It's automatically assigned to the default System Administrator user and provides access to ACLs and High Security Settings. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/c_ElevatedPrivilege.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Elevated privilege on the admin role isn't supported.
impersonator allows impersonating users; it isn't elevated by default.
itil_admin isn't an elevated role.

source.excerpt: In the base system, the security_admin role is the only role that has elevated privileges.

questions.question: Why is assigning roles to groups preferred over assigning them to individual users?

options.text: Group members inherit the role, and a user who switches groups automatically gets the new group's roles
It is the only way to grant roles
Roles assigned to groups never expire, but user roles do
Group roles bypass ACLs

explanation.correct: When you assign roles to groups instead of individual users, group members inherit the role. When a user switches groups, the new group's role is assigned automatically. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/user-administration/t_AssignRoleToGroup.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Roles can also be assigned directly to users.
Expiry doesn't depend on group vs user assignment.
Roles never bypass ACLs; ACLs evaluate roles.

documentation.section: Assign a role to a group

source.excerpt: When you assign roles to groups rather than to individual users, members of the group inherit the role.

questions.question: An administrator impersonates a user and updates a record. How is the update recorded?

options.text: As if the impersonated user made it
As made by the administrator
As made by the System user
It isn't recorded

explanation.correct: During impersonation, the administrator accesses the system exactly as the impersonated user, and all actions are recorded as if the impersonated user performed them. Impersonate Begin and Impersonate End events are logged in the system log. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/user-administration/c_ImpersonateAUser.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Actions are attributed to the impersonated user.
The System user isn't used for impersonation.
Actions are recorded.

source.excerpt: All actions performed by the administrator during impersonation are recorded as if they were executed by the impersonated user.

questions.question: What is the maximum duration of a time-limited role assignment for a user?

options.text: 5 days
24 hours
30 days
There is no limit

explanation.correct: Time-limited roles give users a role for a defined period and remove it automatically. Supported roles include admin, snc_read_only, impersonator, and snc_required_script_writer_permission. A user can have up to four concurrent time-limited roles, each lasting up to 5 days. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/user-administration/time-limited-role-overview.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The documented limit is 5 days.
The documented limit is 5 days.
A maximum is documented.

source.excerpt: Time-limited role can be maximum of 5 days per user.

questions.question: What does ServiceNow recommend when a specialized role, such as business_rule_admin, is available?

options.text: Avoid granting the admin role and grant the more specialized role
Always grant admin so the user has full access
Rename the role to match the job title
Grant both roles to be safe

explanation.correct: Special administrative roles grant specific administrative rights without the full privileges of admin. The guidance is to avoid granting admin when more specialized roles are available. Roles can't be renamed. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/user-administration/r_SpecialAdministrativeRoles.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Least privilege favors the specialized role.
You can't rename roles in the ServiceNow AI Platform.
Granting admin as well defeats the purpose of the specialized role.

source.excerpt: Avoid granting an admin role when more specialized roles are available.

questions.question: In Security Center, what does the hardening compliance score represent?

options.text: A percentage showing how closely your security settings match the recommended settings
The number of security incidents this month
The number of users with the admin role
The percentage of ACLs with scripts

explanation.correct: The hardening compliance score is a percentage that shows how closely your security settings align with the recommended settings. Security Center shows the current score and its history on the instance. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/security-center/homepage.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Security incidents aren't what the score measures.
Admin counts are not the hardening score.
The score isn't based on ACL scripts.

source.excerpt: The hardening compliance score is a percentage that shows how closely your security settings align with the recommended settings.

questions.question: Which Security Center tool scans the instance against a set of security checks to find misconfiguration and lets you build suites of checks for different use cases?

options.text: Security scanner
Customer Actions
Security hardening
My Security Tasks

explanation.correct: The Security scanner scans the instance against security checks to identify misconfiguration and makes it easier to create different suites of checks for different use cases. Customer Actions implements important security updates, and Security hardening shows the compliance score and settings. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/security-center/homepage.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Customer Actions helps implement important security updates.
Security hardening shows the compliance score and hardening settings.
My Security Tasks lists security tasks assigned to you.

source.excerpt: Scan your instance against a set of security checks to identify misconfiguration.

questions.question: Which sections are on the Security Center landing page? (Choose three.)

options.text: Posture
Access management
Monitoring
Update Set Preview
Transform Maps

explanation.correct: The Security Center landing page includes an instance summary, My Security Tasks, Posture, Access management, Machine identity, Other configuration tools, and Monitoring. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/security-center/sec-center-landing.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Update set preview is part of update set management.
Transform maps are part of System Import Sets.

source.excerpt: Use information in the Posture section … View access issues and misconfiguration on your instance … Monitor and detect potential security threats on your instance

questions.question: Which Security Posture Console best practice helps prevent unwanted access by enforcing a default deny posture, including for ServiceNow personnel, who must then explicitly request access?

options.text: Activate the ServiceNow Access Control plugin
Disable browser SQL messages
Enable table auditing
Configure SPF for email

explanation.correct: The ServiceNow Access Control plugin controls which employees can access your instance, and when, by enforcing a default deny posture for all users except those you specify, including ServiceNow employees. Personnel must then request access on an ad-hoc, temporary basis. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/security-center/best-practices.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Disabling SQL messages hides error details from attackers.
Table auditing tracks record changes.
SPF lets your email systems accept mail from the instance.

source.excerpt: After ServiceNow Access Control is activated, personnel must explicitly request access from you on an ad-hoc and temporary basis.

questions.question: Under the ServiceNow Shared Responsibility Model, which statement is correct?

options.text: The customer, as data controller, decides access rights to its instance and data; ServiceNow, as data processor, secures the platform infrastructure
ServiceNow decides who in the customer's organization can access each record
The customer is responsible for securing ServiceNow data center hardware
ServiceNow configures every customer ACL

explanation.correct: ServiceNow describes security as a partnership in which each party has specific responsibilities. As data controller, the customer decides access rights to its instance and data and uses in-instance security controls to implement its policies. As data processor, ServiceNow secures the platform infrastructure and provides tools for security management and monitoring. See https://www.servicenow.com/content/dam/servicenow-assets/public/en-us/doc-type/resource-center/ebook/ebk-how-servicenow-delivers-safe-and-secure-cloud-services.pdf

wrongAnswers.explanation: Access rights within the instance are the customer's responsibility.
Infrastructure security is ServiceNow's responsibility, with its colocation and cloud providers.
Customers configure access controls in their own instances.

documentation.section: Securing the ServiceNow AI Platform (ServiceNow ebook)

source.excerpt: As the data controller, the customer determines access rights to their instance and the data it contains.

questions.question: Where does ServiceNow's Security Center Best Practices list point customers to understand their shared role in keeping their instances secure?

options.text: The Shared Responsibility Model, which defines the partnership between ServiceNow and the customer
The CSDM Foundation domain
The Knowledge Management workflow
The Service Catalog user criteria

explanation.correct: The Best Practices list includes 'Review the Shared Security Model', which tells customers to review the Shared Responsibility Model to understand their role. The model defines a partnership between ServiceNow and the customer in which each has specific responsibilities. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/security-center/best-practices.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: CSDM is a data model for the CMDB.
Knowledge workflows govern article publishing.
User criteria control catalog access.

source.excerpt: The Shared Responsibility Model defines the partnership between and the customer, both with specific responsibilities.

questions.question: Which of these is a customer responsibility, rather than ServiceNow's, when securing an instance? (Choose two.)

options.text: Changing the default passwords on built-in accounts such as admin
Deciding which users get which roles and data access in the instance
Physically securing the data center hosting the instance
Patching the hypervisors in ServiceNow's cloud

explanation.correct: Customers, as data controllers, determine access rights to their instance and data. The Security Center Best Practices also tell customers to change the default passwords on built-in accounts such as admin, ITIL, and employee. Infrastructure security belongs to ServiceNow and its providers. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/security-center/best-practices.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Physical data center security belongs to ServiceNow and its colocation providers.
Platform infrastructure is secured by ServiceNow as data processor.

source.excerpt: Change the passwords on your instance's built-in user accounts, such as admin, ITIL, and employee.

questions.question: An administrator needs an ACL on the Incident table that applies only to incidents with Critical priority. Which ACL field should they use?

options.text: Applies To
Admin overrides
Description
Protection Policy

explanation.correct: The Applies To field adds a filter condition for the table in the Name field, so the ACL applies only to matching records. For example, an ACL on incident can apply only to Critical priority incidents. If Applies To is empty, the ACL applies to all records. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/access-control/t_CreateAnACLRule.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Admin overrides lets admins pass the ACL automatically.
Description only documents the ACL.
Protection Policy sets the ACL's protection level, not which records it applies to.

source.excerpt: For example, you could create an ACL for the incident table that applies only to incidents with the Critical priority.

questions.question: What does a user need before they can grant the security_admin role to other users?

options.text: The admin role, plus elevation to security_admin
Only the admin role
Only the user_admin role
The itil role and group manager status

explanation.correct: To grant security_admin, the granting user must have the admin role and must elevate to security_admin first. A user with only the admin role can't grant security_admin, and a user with only user_admin can't grant admin. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/c_ElevatedPrivilege.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Admin alone can't grant security_admin.
user_admin can't grant admin or security_admin.
itil doesn't allow granting privileged roles.

source.excerpt: A user with only the admin role cannot grant the security_admin role to other users.

questions.question: When an administrator creates a new table, what does selecting the Create access controls check box do?

options.text: No security is applied by default
Creates basic security rules (access controls) for the table, using the role entered in the User role field
Only admin users can access the table
The table is marked as read-only

explanation.correct: On the table creation form, selecting Create access controls and filling in the User role field creates basic security rules for the new table. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/t_CreateATable.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: ServiceNow automatically creates baseline access controls for new tables.
Access depends on the automatically created ACLs, not just admin restrictions.
New tables are not automatically read-only; access is controlled by ACLs.

source.excerpt: Select the check box and then complete the User role field to create basic security rules for the table.

questions.question: A user passes a table-level ACL but fails a field-level ACL. What access does the user have?

options.text: Full access to the record including all fields
No access to the record at all
Access to the record but not to that specific field
Read-only access to all fields

explanation.correct: Access controls are checked in order, starting with table access and then field access. Failing a table rule denies access to all. Passing a table rule but failing a field rule denies access to that field only. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The user would be denied access to the specific field that failed the ACL check.
Table-level access was granted, so the user can see the record, just not the restricted field.
The field restriction is specific to the failed ACL, not a global read-only state.

source.excerpt: Access controls are checked in order, starting with table access and then field access. Failing a table rule denies access to all passing a table rule, but failing a field rule denies access to that field.

questions.question: What does an upward arrow next to a user's avatar indicate in ServiceNow?

options.text: The user has unread notifications
The user has activated elevated privileges
The user is impersonating another user
The user has pending approvals

explanation.correct: An upward arrow next to your avatar indicates activated elevated privileges. This visual indicator helps administrators know when they have temporary elevated security access. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Unread notifications are indicated differently, typically with a badge number.
Impersonation is indicated by a different visual cue showing the impersonated user.
Pending approvals appear in the approval modules, not as avatar indicators.

source.excerpt: An upward arrow next to your avatar indicates activated elevated privileges.

questions.question: What limitation applies to users with the admin role when impersonating another user?

options.text: They cannot impersonate any users
They can only impersonate users in their group
They cannot impersonate the security_admin role or elevate privileges during impersonation
They must have manager approval to impersonate

explanation.correct: Admins cannot impersonate the security admin role or elevate privileges during impersonation to access high security functions. This is a security measure to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive security configurations. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Admins can impersonate other users, but with certain restrictions.
Impersonation is not limited to group membership for admins.
Manager approval is not required for admin impersonation by default.

source.excerpt: However, admins cannot impersonate the security admin role or elevate privileges during impersonation to access high security functions.

questions.question: Which components does ServiceNow use to ensure security for CRUD operations? (Choose two.)

options.text: User authentication/login managed via users, groups, and roles
Automatic data encryption at rest
Application and module access controlled by roles
Mandatory two-factor authentication

explanation.correct: ServiceNow ensures security for CRUD operations with: user authentication/login managed via users, groups and roles; application and module access controlled by roles; and database access managed by system properties and table/field access controls. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: While encryption may be available, it's not one of the core CRUD security mechanisms described.
MFA is an optional security feature, not a core CRUD operation security mechanism.

source.excerpt: ServiceNow ensures security for CRUD operations with, user authentication/login, managed via users, groups and roles, application and module access controlled by roles.

questions.question: A system administrator needs to grant a user temporary elevated access to modify ACLs. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Permanently assign the security_admin role to the user
Have the user activate elevated privileges for their session
Give the user the admin role
Disable all ACLs temporarily

explanation.correct: Elevated privileges allow temporary access to higher security functions and last only for the current session. This is more secure than permanently assigning roles because access automatically ends with logout, timeout, or impersonation. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Permanently assigning security_admin violates the principle of least privilege for temporary needs.
Admin role alone doesn't grant ACL modification - security_admin is still required.
Disabling ACLs would create significant security risks and is not recommended.

source.excerpt: Elevated roles allow modification of the access control list. These roles last only for your session.

questions.question: Which statements about the admin role in ServiceNow are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Admins have access to all platform features and can override access controls
Admins can automatically modify ACLs without any additional roles
The admin role should be assigned cautiously
Admins can impersonate security_admin during impersonation sessions

explanation.correct: Admins have access to all platform features and can override access controls, so the role should be assigned cautiously. However, admins cannot modify ACLs without security_admin and cannot impersonate security_admin during impersonation. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=400ce92b47530e10123f3975d36d43f1&child_id=8a89ef9447735ad4ca332a81736d432f&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Admins need the security_admin role in addition to admin to modify ACLs.
Admins cannot impersonate security_admin or elevate privileges during impersonation.

source.excerpt: Admins have access to all platform features and can override access controls so assign this role cautiously.

questions.question: A user has the catalog_admin role. What access does this provide?

options.text: Only access to the Service Catalog application
Only access to user criteria modules
Access to all Service Catalog and user criteria modules, plus additional catalog_admin permissions
Full admin access to all platform features

explanation.correct: The catalog_admin role includes permissions from both user_criteria_admin and catalog roles, providing access to all applications and modules of both roles plus any permissions specific to catalog_admin. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/user-administration/r_BaseSystemRoles.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: catalog_admin includes more than just the catalog role — it also contains user_criteria_admin permissions.
catalog_admin includes user criteria access but also catalog and additional permissions.
catalog_admin provides access to catalog-related features, not full admin access.

source.excerpt: Catalog administrators can manage the Service Catalog application, including catalog categories and items. Contains Roles: user_criteria_admin, catalog_builder_editor, catalog_template_editor, catalog, catalog_lookup_admin

questions.question: What is the purpose of the ServiceNow Security Center?

options.text: To manage user passwords and authentication only
To monitor security compliance, manage hardening settings, and run security scans
To configure firewalls and network security
To create and manage encryption keys

explanation.correct: ServiceNow Security Center is a built-in tool that helps system administrators manage and improve instance security. It includes hardening checks, security scanning, customer actions, notifications, and compliance scoring. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-security/security-center/homepage.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Security Center covers much more than passwords — it includes hardening, scanning, compliance, and metrics.
Security Center focuses on instance security settings, not network infrastructure.
Encryption key management is not the primary purpose of Security Center.

source.excerpt: Use the security configuration page to get an overview of the security posture of your instance. View your hardening compliance score, discover graphical trends, analyze the top non-compliant hardening settings, and see the results of your security scans.

questions.question: What does role delegation allow in ServiceNow?

options.text: Designated users (role delegators) can assign roles they already have to other users within a group
Automatically assigning admin roles to all managers
Delegating system upgrades to non-admin users
Sharing admin credentials with a team

explanation.correct: Administrators can let users assign roles within groups. These role delegators can only assign roles they already have. The role_delegator role can be granted manually, or automatically to group managers through the Group Manager Change business rule. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/australia/platform-administration/user-administration/c_DelegateRoles.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Delegated administration is a targeted permission, not automatic role assignment to managers.
System upgrades require full admin access and cannot be delegated this way.
Sharing credentials violates security best practices and is not what delegated administration means.

source.excerpt: Administrators can grant users the ability to assign roles within groups. However, these users can only assign roles that they already have.
